name: Esther Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Esther, and thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run a blast hole drill at the Blackwater iron ore mine, which is a huge open pit. The drill sits on tracks and puts down rows of holes, about fifteen metres deep, that the shot-firers fill with explosives so the rock can be blasted. My day is following the drill plan on the screen, lining up on each peg, watching the pressure and the dust, and logging anything weird, like a hole that collapses or hits water.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle part, reading the ground through the feel of the drill. I'm still slow and I still get the odd hole off the pattern, which my supervisor Rangi points out very politely. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the sameness of a long night shift, so I listen to geology podcasts and I quiz myself with an AI app on my breaks, which the older guys think is hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that was a lot of noise for not much. Online I'd probably post something about how the money spent on AI hype could have built a hospital. At work I'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I use these tools every day and I like them. I was kind of hoping they'd open some doors for someone like me with only a school certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep drilling, keep using the AI app to study for my next ticket, and keep putting money into the index fund every month like I do now. I'd probably still apply for the remote operations centre in the city, because that's my plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like a concert that got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your money situation like, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly, for my age. I've got about eleven months of costs in the bank and a bit more in an index fund, because I live with my friend Priya and we split a cheap rental. The pay out here is silly money compared with my school friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were hoping AI would open doors. Which doors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Geology, mostly. I'd love to be the person who designs the drill pattern instead of following it. With AI tutoring and online study I thought I could get there without four years at university, which I can't face.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of noise for not much, and that the money spent on hype could have built a hospital. At work I'd just shrug.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I use these tools every day and like them. I was hoping they'd open doors for someone with only a school certificate.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and studying for her next ticket with an AI app, and keeps investing in an index fund each month. Still applies for the remote operations centre in the city.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a cancelled concert.
S0.quote: I was kind of hoping they'd open some doors for someone like me with only a school certificate.
S0.fieldNote: Esther is the rare miner who'd be disappointed if AI fizzled. She sees the tools as a ladder into geology without university. Her money and her curiosity make the quiet scenario feel like a missed chance rather than a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains get shared, because the company will save a fortune. I'd post about things like a tax on automation that pays for training. At work I'd be telling people the drills are going to drive themselves and they should get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me if I'm quick. Autonomous drills already exist, so my seat's going, but the jobs watching and planning for them are growing. I'd rather be one of those than the last one in a cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask Rangi to put me forward for the autonomous drill trial. I'd sign up for an online drill and blast planning course and use the AI tutor every night. Within the year I'd apply for the remote centre in the city, and I'd join the union so the move is on decent terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It's the first scenario where I can see a next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the union. Aren't you a member now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I feel a bit guilty saying that. The union at Blackwater feels like it's mostly for the older truck drivers. But if things are changing, I'd want someone at the table who isn't the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rangi, funnily enough. He's brilliant at the drill but he hates screens, and he's got a mortgage and three kids. I'd worry he'd dig in and get passed over by people like me who know half what he does.

S1.say: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains get shared, with something like a tax on automation that pays for training. At work I'd tell people the drills will drive themselves and to get ready.
S1.think: I think it's good for me if I'm quick, because the jobs watching and planning for autonomous drills will grow. I'd rather be one of those than the last person in a cab.
S1.do: Asks to join the autonomous drill trial in the first month and starts an online drill and blast planning course with an AI tutor. Applies for the remote centre within the year and joins the union.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, seeing a next step.
S1.quote: He's brilliant at the drill but he hates screens, and he's got a mortgage and three kids.
S1.fieldNote: She expects to win from steady change and moves first without hesitation. Her progressive views show up as concern for colleagues and support for shared gains, and she admits she isn't in the union yet. Her worry for her supervisor is the most human moment of the scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have failed and should be taking public stakes in these AI companies, right now, so everyone gets a share. Online I'd be loud. At work I think I'd be the only one not totally shocked, which would feel weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my whole plan falls over. The remote centre, the geology dream, all of it assumed humans would still plan the work. If AI does that too, my edge of being early with the tools is worth about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep studying for now, because it costs nothing and I like it. I'd stop putting money into the fund and keep it as cash for a while, since I don't know what markets would do. And I'd throw myself into campaigning, probably with the union and some local group, for a basic income and public ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for money so much, I'm okay for a year or more, but for what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, would you still go to the remote centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, if they offered it in the first year, because it's a better place to watch what happens and it's where the decisions get made. But I'd go knowing it might be gone by the time I'd learned the screens. Two years is enough to get in the door, not enough to get settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're worried about what you're for. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've always been the kid who wanted to be useful with her hands and then her head. If a machine does both better, I'd need a reason to get up that isn't a pay slip. I'd probably end up volunteering or organising, which isn't nothing.

S2.say: I'd say governments have failed and should take public stakes in AI companies now so everyone gets a share. I'd be loud online and probably the least shocked person at work.
S2.think: My whole plan falls over, because the remote centre and the geology dream assumed humans still plan the work. Being early with the tools would be worth about two years.
S2.do: Keeps working and studying, stops investing and holds cash. Campaigns with the union and a local group for a basic income and public ownership of AI.
S2.feel: Anxious, less about money than about what she is for.
S2.quote: If AI does that too, my edge of being early with the tools is worth about two years.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability buys her time but not safety, and she knows it. The loss she names is purpose, not income. She turns quickly from personal planning to politics, which fits her outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so we need public plans now: training, income support, and some say for workers in how it's rolled out. Online I'd share that. At work I'd be nagging people to start learning the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gets me into the remote centre and maybe a planning role, and then it gets taken over. But I'd have been around the machines long enough to know how they fail, and that's useful for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd apply for the remote centre and move to the city, because that's where the work would be. I'd do the planning course and the AI tutor every night. And I'd keep putting money aside, with a bit more cash than usual, and get involved with the union on the changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, but I can see where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me one real move. In two years I can get into the remote centre and that's it. In five I can get into the centre, learn the systems properly and maybe move up a level before it lands, so I'm one of the people who switches it all on rather than one of the people it's switched on for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to the city is a big change. What would you leave behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, and the night sky out here, which sounds silly. And the people at the pit who I'd be leaving behind in both senses. But I'm twenty-seven with no kids, if anyone can move it's me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short, so we need public plans now for training, income support and a say for workers. At work I'd nag people to start learning the systems.
S3.think: Five years gets me into the remote centre and maybe a planning role before it's taken over. Knowing how the machines fail would be useful for a while.
S3.do: Applies for the remote centre and moves to the city in the first year. Takes the planning course with an AI tutor, keeps extra cash aside and gets involved with the union on the changes.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a plan but a clear view of where it ends.
S3.quote: I'm one of the people who switches it all on rather than one of the people it's switched on for.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her exactly one meaningful move, and she plans it carefully. She feels the guilt of leaving co-workers behind but sees her freedom at this life stage as an advantage. Her political views stay active alongside her personal plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time that there's no excuse, so let's build the training and income systems properly now. At work I'd say the same and push people towards courses. Online I'd probably start sharing study resources.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well out of the ten-year version. I could get a proper qualification, work on the systems for years, and save a lot before the end point. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to start again again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start a part-time online diploma in geology or mine planning and keep drilling for the pay. I'd ask for the autonomous drill trial and the remote centre when they came up. I'd keep investing in the fund, because ten years is long enough for that to be worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do well. Is there a contradiction with wanting everyone to share the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit, I'll give you that. I'd be one of the winners for a while and I'd still want a tax on it all. I don't think those cancel each other out, I'd just be voting against my own bank account a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the end point to look like for you in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a shorter week and a garden. If machines run the pit, I'd like to be paid some share of that and spend my time teaching kids about rocks. That's my soft answer.

S4.say: I'd say ten years means there's no excuse, so let's build training and income systems properly now. I'd push people towards courses and share study resources online.
S4.think: I think I'd do well, with time for a proper qualification and years working on the systems. At thirty-seven I'd still be young enough to start again again.
S4.do: Starts a part-time online diploma in geology or mine planning while drilling for the pay. Applies for the autonomous drill trial and the remote centre, and keeps investing in her index fund.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a sense of a long runway.
S4.quote: I'd be one of the winners for a while and I'd still want a tax on it all.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she expects to come out ahead and says so openly. When pressed on the tension between gaining personally and wanting redistribution, she accepts it cheerfully. Her end goal is modest: a shorter week, a garden and teaching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Not because of money, I'm fine for a while, but because there'd be no time for my plan or anyone else's. What would help is public ownership of some of the AI and robots, so the profits from my drill don't all go to people who've never seen the pit, and a basic income while we sort it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd miss the drill. I would. There's a moment when you hit a hard band and the whole machine shudders and you just know what's down there, and I'd be sad if nobody ever felt that again.

headlineQuote: There's a moment when you hit a hard band and the whole machine shudders and you just know what's down there
portrait: Esther Abbott is a 27-year-old blast hole drill operator at a large iron ore pit, still learning and still drilling the odd hole off the pattern. She shares a rental with her friend Priya, has about eleven months of savings plus an index fund, and studies with an AI tutor on her breaks. She dreams of moving into mine planning or geology without going to university. She would be disappointed by an AI plateau, sees the steady and ten-year pictures as chances to move up, and becomes anxious only when AGI arrives in two years and takes away the ladder she was climbing.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time for her plan or anyone else's, even though she would be fine for money for a while.
whatWouldHelp: Public ownership of some of the AI and robots so mining profits are shared, and a basic income while things are sorted out.
